Cotton Mather
kot'ūn math'êr
n. (Cotton Mather, 1663–1728, Boston minister and author of Magnalia Christi Americana, the most prolific writer of colonial New England)
Cotton, his mother's family name, from John Cotton; Mather, from Old English, a mower.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Cotton Mather entered Harvard at eleven, assisted and then succeeded his father at Boston's North Church, and published some four hundred and fifty works. His Magnalia Christi Americana of 1702 is the great ecclesiastical history of New England; his Bonifacius, an essay on doing good, shaped Franklin's youth by Franklin's own account. He was a fellow of the Royal Society and in 1721 pressed the Boston physicians to inoculate against smallpox, having learned of the practice from Onesimus, an African member of his household; the city rioted and a bomb was thrown through his window. He also wrote in support of the Salem prosecutions at a time when his father was writing against them, and that stain is permanent. Jas 5:16 lies behind the pastoral diaries he kept. Mat 5:16 is the text of Bonifacius, that men may see good works and glorify the Father. Pro 11:30 names the aim of the whole output.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines inoculation as the act or practice of communicating a disease to a person in health, by inserting contagious matter in his skin; and beneficence, as the practice of doing good.

expand to see more

INOCULA'TION, n. The act or practice of communicating a disease to a person in health, by inserting contagious matter in his skin or flesh.

BENEF'ICENCE, n. The practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity.

POLYG'RAPHY, n. Much writing; the art of writing in various unusual manners.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:16 — "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."

Jas 5:16 — "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much."

Pro 11:30 — "The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise."

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Modern Corruption

He faced a mob to defend inoculation and defended the Salem court, and both belong in the same paragraph.

expand to see more

Mather's career refuses to be simplified, and the dictionary does not try. The man who risked his house to save Boston from smallpox is the same man who lent his pen to a court convicting neighbours on dreams. Mat 5:16 ties good works to the glory of the Father rather than to the reputation of the doer, which is the measure that lets both facts stand without either cancelling the other.

The modern handling of Mather is the corruption worth naming. He is used as a caricature of Puritan cruelty by writers who have read neither Bonifacius nor the inoculation pamphlets, and as an unblemished hero by admirers who skip 1692. Jas 1:27 and Jas 5:16 describe a religion of visiting the afflicted and confessing faults one to another, and a historian who will not let a subject do both has not understood Christian biography.

Usage

"“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — the text of Bonifacius."

"“Confess your faults one to another” (Jas 5:16) — a duty he preached and partly discharged."

"“he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — the aim of four hundred books."
